entries.title: How to teach with Databricks Free Edition
entries.summary: You can run a full data or AI course on the same platform enterprises use in production - for free...
entries.content:
A practical guide for faculty: map your courses to the right tools, distribute assignments, and get students building on real production data and AI infrastructure, for free.

by Joey Frazee and Elise Hollowed

  • One platform can support an entire data + AI curriculum, from introductory data science and statistics through data engineering, BI, machine learning, AI, and capstone projects.
  • The learning experience is closer to real-world practice: students use Apache Spark, Delta Lake, MLflow, Lakebase, Genie, Databricks Apps, and other industry tools rather than learning a separate classroom-only stack.
  • Adoption is designed to be lightweight for instructors: assignments can be distributed through an existing LMS or GitHub, students can collaborate in shared notebooks, and datasets can be distributed through cloud storage, Open Sharing, or Marketplace.

You can run a full data or AI course on the same platform enterprises use in production - for free, with no cloud contract, no license to manage, and nothing to install. Databricks Free Edition is a perpetually free version of the platform; each student signs up individually and works entirely in the browser, so a course can adopt it without provisioning servers or purchasing anything.

Data and AI skills are moving faster than most curricula can follow, and the demand for these skills is showing up in both hiring and learner behavior. LinkedIn named Databricks one of its Top 10 Skills on the Rise for 2026, while Udemy included Databricks among its 100 Fastest-Growing Global Skills. Two very different signals pointing in the same direction: knowing how to work with modern data and AI platforms is increasingly valuable.

For a student, that can be the difference between “I've studied distributed computing” and “I've built a data pipeline on the platform your team uses.” For an instructor, it means making an existing course more directly connected to how data and AI work gets done in industry, without fully redesigning the curriculum.

The barriers that often make industry platforms difficult to bring into the classroom, including cost, licensing, and IT provisioning, are solved by Databricks Free Edition; a permanently free account with no credit card, no cloud contract, and nothing to install.

That matters because the two usual barriers to teaching with industry tools are cost and setup, and Free Edition removes both. It’s designed specifically for learning and non-commercial use, and is available to students and educators globally.

What is Databricks Free Edition? A no-cost, perpetually free version of the Databricks Data + AI Platform, built for students, hobbyists, and aspiring data and AI professionals. It runs in the browser with no cloud contract and no credit card required to sign up, on smaller compute sizes under fair-use limits. It is not for production or commercial use. (Source: databricks.com/learn/free-edition)

Databricks also has deep roots in academia. It was founded by the UC Berkeley professors and PhD students who created Apache Spark™, and open source is still at the center of what we build - Delta Lake, MLflow, and Unity Catalog are developed with global communities under vendor-neutral foundations (the Linux Foundation, LF AI & Data, and the Apache Software Foundation), and Databricks recently open sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness for AI agents. For educators, that means the skills students build are rooted in industry-wide open standards, not a single proprietary tool.

Because Free Edition is the real platform rather than a simplified sandbox, the skills transfer directly. A student who writes a Spark job, runs a SQL query, deploys a model, or builds an agent in Free Edition is using the same tools professionals use in production. There's no "now unlearn the training tool and learn the real one" step later.

One environment can serve as a statistics lab, a database course, a business-analytics class, and an AI capstone - which cuts the number of tools students and instructors have to learn. This table maps common courses to the tools that might fit your current curriculum.

Capstones, software-engineering projects, student builds and hackathons Databricks Apps Build and deploy interactive data and AI applications Building Enterprise Applications with Databricks Apps

Across these surfaces, Genie Code, the platform's agentic coding and data assistant, helps students generate, explain, and debug code and take on multi-step tasks autonomously, reflecting how work is increasingly done.

Distribute through your existing LMS or a GitHub repository. Export the assignment notebook as an 

.ipynb
file and share it with any datasets or instructions; students import a copy into their Free Edition workspace, complete it, and export the finished notebook for submission. For group assignments, students can share a notebook and collaborate in real time.

Three options for datasets too large for GitHub or a local download: (1) host the dataset in cloud storage students connect to; (2) use Open Sharing to share the dataset from your Free Edition workspace directly into each student's workspace; or (3) pick a free dataset from Databricks Marketplace that students access natively inside the platform.

Yes. Databricks is built for collaboration — with real-time co-authoring, comments, and tagging, students can work together and invite you into their notebooks to troubleshoot or give feedback. Databricks Free Edition is designed for up to five people to share an account for a group project. See how to set up collaboration in Databricks Free Edition.

Free Edition runs on smaller compute sizes under fair-use limits. If a workspace exceeds its quota, its compute pauses for the rest of the day and resumes the next day. Hitting a limit mid-assignment is rare and never permanent. Furthermore, you and your students can double your available daily credit up to three times per year, so students can always keep working during crunch periods and exams. The best way to ensure a smooth experience is to test each assignment in Free Edition ahead of time to catch any step that needs significant compute.

Yes - it's perpetually free, with no cloud contract and no credit card required to sign up. It's built for learning and explicitly not for production or commercial use, which fits a classroom well. Credits reset daily, so students start each day fresh.

A good place to start is anywhere you currently use a cloud-based notebook environment. Sign up for Databricks Free Edition yourself and take the Databricks Fundamentals course; once you're comfortable, assign both to your students and see how the self-paced courses fit your existing curriculum.

entries.title: Building live intelligence: Databricks AI Search supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg
entries.summary: AI Search now natively supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed...
entries.content:
by Yu-Ju Huang, Ankit Vij, Vadim Antonov and Dima Kotlyarov

  • AI Search natively supports three new table sources in addition to Delta tables: Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg v3+.
  • Use AI search to support real-time intelligence, personalized experiences, and cross-engine AI applications.
  • Use the same AI Search workflow across data sources, from the UI or API, without building separate synchronization pipelines.

AI Search now natively supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg v3+ in addition to Delta tables. You can bring live events, continuously maintained personalized state, and open-format data directly into your AI Search applications — reducing the overhead of building and managing separate pipelines to convert and synchronize these data sources.

Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed Iceberg each represent a different way of working with data, and each opens up new possibilities for AI applications.

Data source Best for What it enables
Delta tables (existing) Data and analytical workloads Broad range of analytics and AI applications
Streaming Tables Continuously arriving events Fraud detection, security monitoring, and real-time IoT analytics
Materialized Views Custom aggregated and joined data Personalization, session-aware search, agent assist
Managed tables using Iceberg Open-format data across engines Cross-engine agents, unified knowledge search, open-format data intelligence

Continuously changing data such as new listings, inventory, availability, and user activity can flow into an append-only Streaming Table, with AI Search indexing new records as they arrive and keeping the search index up to date. This freshness enables applications where the latest data can directly shape the search experience: helping users discover newly available restaurants through a search bar, or generating real-time recommendations based on recent trends.

Materialized Views can aggregate events, filter records, and join data from multiple sources to create customized state. As the underlying data changes, the view is incrementally maintained and AI Search propagates those changes to the index, enabling personalized search experiences such as session-aware recommendations, product and content discovery based on recent activity, or tailor results to a user's evolving interests and preferences.

Managed Iceberg tables can serve as AI Search sources directly, without conversion or migration to another table format, making open-format data available to search indexes and other AI applications. The open-format enables AI applications that work across existing data environments: search across product catalogs managed by different systems, unify business or customer data stored across Managed Iceberg tables, or build search experiences over large, distributed datasets without moving the underlying data.

Before native support, customers had to create a separate Delta representation of Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, or Managed Iceberg tables and build pipelines to keep it synchronized with the source. This added an extra data layer, custom update logic, and ongoing operational overhead.

Now, AI Search connects directly to these sources. Create an index from your source and sync it when needed — AI Search propagates them directly to the index, eliminating the intermediate Delta table and custom synchronization pipeline. Your data stays connected to search as it evolves, with the platform handling the plumbing behind the scenes.

Whether you use the UI or API, building an AI Search index follows the same workflow used for existing Delta table sources: create a Delta Sync index and point it at your source table. The same workflow now extends to Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Iceberg tables — no new workflow to learn.

Ready to build AI applications on your data? Get started by creating an AI Search index directly from your Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, or Managed Iceberg tables — no additional data pipelines required. Explore the AI Search documentation.

entries.title: The media industry is becoming a prediction economy
entries.summary: For two decades, media and advertising ran on attention. Impressions, reach and clicks...
entries.content:
What it takes to make predictive intelligence in marketing and advertising a reality

by Elena Tesser

• The prediction economy is the shift in media and advertising from counting attention to predicting and proving outcomes. Performance becomes a leading indicator instead of a lagging one.

• Agents and measurement stall on fragmented data. Only 3% of CMOs can tie half their marketing to a business outcome (McKinsey), and the fix is one unified, governed data and AI foundation.

• Build it on four Cs: context (Databricks CustomerLake, an agentic CDP; Genie; Lakebase), control, cost, and choice (Unity Gateway). A pet specialty retailer that activated loyalty data with agents saw a 12% lift in transactions.

For two decades, media and advertising ran on attention. Impressions, reach and clicks were the currency because they were quantifiable. Increasingly, though, that currency is losing value. Throughout the industry – and brought to a head at Advertising Week New York – leaders across media, agencies, and adtech/martech are asking the same question: not "who saw it?" but "what did it change?"

Behind every answer is the rise of the prediction economy, where advantage comes from knowing what an audience will want before the money is spent, and being able to show what it was worth. Performance has shifted from a lagging indicator to a leading one.

Hear Databricks Media and Advertising GTM leader Jake LaDuke share his thoughts on the prediction economy - and the future of media, advertising and marketing - then read on to learn more.

A few themes deserving attention:

Agents are moving from answering to acting. Session after session, conversation after conversation on agentic AI reaches the same conclusion: agents fail without trusted, governed data underneath them. The early wins are as much about effectiveness as efficiency, such as orchestrating measurement across many sources of truth. On the sell side, roles like VP of ad sales transformation barely existed two years ago, as agents take over the spreadsheets, emails and stale rate cards of pitch-to-pay so sellers can focus on relationships and yield.

Measurement has to prove impact. According to a McKinsey study, only 3% of CMOs can tie half their marketing to a business outcome. That mandate is rippling through the ecosystem: agencies are restructuring contracts, adtech is building proof into its products, and publishers are launching their own measurement. The hope economy is giving way to the prediction economy, and the loop only closes if partner data can connect.

Martech and adtech are collapsing into one stack. With 90 to 120 tools in a typical enterprise stack, channel-level reporting no longer cuts it. CMOs need holistic performance across every touchpoint, not just advertising or marketing alone. Meanwhile CMOs and CROs draw on the same audiences from separate stacks, and collapsing the two lets both do better.

CTV and retail media need closed loops. Publishers need one data estate for audience intelligence, monetization and cross-platform measurement. Retail media, a fast-growing channel still held back by measurement, needs clean rooms, first-party activation and closed-loop measurement.

Behind all of it, consumer behavior is shifting faster than the stack. Agentic commerce, AI-generated creative and LLMs acting as the new influencer are changing how people discover brands, and executives want to treat these shifts as opportunities, not threats.

Every one of these points back to the same prerequisite: a unified, governed data and AI foundation. When your data is fragmented, adapting to the prediction economy becomes untenable. Leaders must stop funding these as separate projects and instead build one foundation for every persona to draw on.

Every prediction starts with context: how complete a view your agents have of your customers and your business across your data estate. As Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi has put it, models don’t have an intelligence problem, they have a context problem.

PetSmart shows what happens when that context comes together. Using loyalty data from its 75 million Treats Rewards members, the company moved beyond batch-and-blast campaigns, and AI decisioning agents delivered personalized messaging at scale. The result was a 22% incremental lift in salon bookings and a 13% lift in auto-ship transactions. The gain came from getting the data estate to work together, not from a smarter model.

Nowhere does context matter more than in the customer 360. Marketers increasingly want to run marketing where they run the business, rather than copying golden profiles into a separate CDP. That is the idea behind CustomerLake, Databricks’ agentic CDP. Marketing and data teams can build trusted Customer 360 profiles, activate audiences and personalize engagement directly on their governed data. Paired with measurement orchestration, those same customer signals connect directly to ROI.

Genie then brings that context to the people making decisions. It acts as an AI coworker connected to your governed enterprise data, so planners, marketers and sellers can ask questions in plain language and get answers built on their own definitions. Under the hood, Genie Ontology gives the AI an understanding of your business: its unique definitions, relationships, business rules, authoritative sources and permissions. At answer or decision time, it ranks that context by authority and relevance, applies permissions, and delivers the most useful pieces.

Acting intelligently in the moment also takes operational context: what the customer just did, what they were offered, and what the agent decided and why. Lakebase, Databricks’ serverless Postgres database, keeps that live state next to your analytical data, so agent memory, decision history and fresh features are available at production speed without brittle pipelines in between.

Getting there starts with a simple discipline: define identity, audiences and metrics once, and govern them centrally.

Context gets you to a prediction. The other three C's decide whether you can afford to act on it at scale, and whether you should.

Control. This is about governing not only who has access from a people perspective, but also from your agents' perspective. Agents will touch audience data, bids and brand-sensitive placements, so governance has to be the front door. Unity Gateway runs every model and agent request through one control plane, with authentication, auditing and PII guardrails, so the enterprise sets the guardrails and the platform enforces them.

Cost. AI for AI's sake is no longer tolerated by CFOs, and the shift is from token maxing to value maxing. Every agent loop burns tokens, and always-on campaigns multiply that. Unity Gateway attributes spend by team, model and application, enforces budgets and rate limits, and routes simple requests to cheaper models, so AI cost tracks business value.

Choice. Having the right model for the right job matters because frontier models leapfrog each other regularly. If switching means rewriting applications, you are always a generation behind. Unity Gateway offers models from multiple providers through one API, so you can swap by configuration instead of re-engineering. Built on open formats, the foundation keeps your data portable, and OpenSharing and Databricks Clean Rooms let you collaborate with partners without copying data

Leaders should treat governance, cost visibility and portability as design requirements from day one, not retrofits.

Looking ahead, advertising itself will change. With ad avoidance rising and intent still largely untapped, it must shift from feeling like a break in what people want to do to a more intelligent, integrated 1:1 experience driven by that viewer’s intent. Getting there will take new operating systems and operating models across brands, agencies, adtech and publishers, all in service of outcomes.

Moving forward, leaders need to think big about how AI can be a growth lever for the business, then aim small on the use cases you unlock first, whether that's audience planning, activation or measurement orchestration. Start with the why: a new revenue stream, lower costs or simpler operations. Not every problem needs an agent.

Pick one meaningful decision, such as reactivating lapsed customers, packaging an audience for a buyer or closing the loop on a retail media campaign. Assemble the context, set the guardrails, agree up front on how you will measure impact, and expand from there. Those who go furthest fastest will be business people growing more technical and technical people growing more business-centric, building on trusted context, real control, the freedom to choose, and costs that scale with value.

Ready to get started? Watch the video with Beet.TV, listen to the podcast with Advertising Week, and learn more at Databricks for Media, Advertising, & Entertainment.

entries.title: Built for Agents: The Case for Spark Declarative Pipelines
entries.summary: AI agents now write a growing share of production data pipelines (over 70% of SDP...
entries.content:
We benchmarked 528 agent-built data pipelines - declarative authoring proved cheaper, faster and leaner than procedural code.

by Lisa Cao and Sudhanva Huruli

  • Procedural pipelines burned about 34x as much compute time as declarative pipelines, primarily because errors in structurally invalid declarative pipelines are caught by a cheap “dry run” which does not fully execute them.
  • Declarative pipelines contain 51% less code for the same pipeline, so there is far less to read and review.
  • Together, these efficiencies make declarative frameworks like SDP the clear architectural choice for autonomous agents building production pipelines.

AI agents now write a growing share of production data pipelines (over 70% of SDP pipelines on Databricks are now created by agents) which raises the stakes in two areas: (1) every attempt an agent makes costs compute and time, so iterations need to be cheap and efficient to run; and (2) code review become a critical gate, so the code needs to be succinct, readable, and correct. Apache Spark® offers two programming models to author your pipelines, procedural and declarative, and they differ in what you write, in what Spark can check before it runs, and in how much a mistake costs. We benchmarked both with the same agent on the same jobs, and declarative came out safer, cheaper, and leaner.

A procedural pipeline is code that tells Spark how to build each dataset, step by step. The only way to know whether it works is to run it.

A declarative pipeline describes the datasets you want and leaves Spark to decide how to build them. This is akin to when you prompt an LLM, and it figures out how to do it (by using the right skills & tools). This is best illustrated in code to see how a simple typo will fail:

Procedural Declarative 
bronze = spark.read.parquet(RAW)
bronze.write.saveAsTable("bronze")
silver = 
bronze.withColumnRenamed("revenue", 
"revenues")  # typo
silver.write.saveAsTable("silver")
gold = 
spark.read.table("silver").groupBy("revenue")
.sum("revenue")
gold.write.saveAsTable("gold")  
# runtime error

@dp.materialized_view(name="gold")
def gold():
    return 
spark.read.table("silver").groupBy("revenue")
.sum("revenue")

Bugs come in two flavors. Structural ones you can catch by reading the pipeline: an unresolved column reference, a table that doesn’t exist yet, a config change that is not allowed. Silent ones only show up in the output when the run finishes and the answer is wrong.

A declarative pipeline can be checked for structural bugs before it runs, similar to how data flow in a typed language like Rust can be checked at compile time. Because a declarative pipeline is a description rather than a run, Spark can answer three kinds of questions by reading it:

  • Every column reference is resolved against the schema of the dataset it reads from, so a column that does not exist is a rejection rather than a runtime failure.
  • Every dependency between datasets is matched to a producer in the graph, so a reference to a table that nothing declares is caught before the pipeline starts.
  • The graph is checked for completeness and ordering, so the engine determines what runs when rather than trusting the order in which the model happened to write things.

In procedural PySpark, the AI coding agent writes the data operations, such as filtering invalid rows and joining tables. It also writes code to run the pipeline’s steps in the right order and save their results. This supporting code repeats much of the same boilerplate across pipelines.

In declarative pipelines, the AI agent defines each dataset and the query that produces it. Spark handles the execution order and saves the results. With Spark handling that boilerplate, the agent writes less code, and the team has less to review and maintain.

We tested 22 data engineering tasks. Each task looked like a real ticket: it described a problem and specified the table, column names, and data types that the pipeline had to produce. The agent could choose any implementation as long as the output matched those requirements.

For each task, we generated 12 different input datasets with the kinds of messy values found in production data. The agent wrote a new pipeline for every dataset using procedural PySpark and another using Spark Declarative Pipelines. That produced 264 builds per approach and 528 in total: 22 tasks × 12 datasets × 2 approaches. All builds used Opus 4.8.

We ran each pipeline and checked its output against the required table. The automated grader did not know which approach had produced the result. Declarative pipelines first went through Spark's dry run. If a build failed, the agent could revise it and try again, up to a fixed limit.

You can rerun the whole thing yourself from the public repository: the setup, prompts, datasets, grader, and the results behind every number.

Both ways finished nearly every task, with 255 of 264 completed procedurally and 258 of 264 completed declaratively, so either one gets you to a working pipeline. What differs is everything around that: when mistakes surfaced, how much code it took to fix, and how consistent the output was. We cover the three advantages of declarative pipelines below, followed by two caveats.

1. Validating before the run made declarative pipelines ~34x less time

A pipeline's mistakes surface before execution, during a run, or not at all. Procedural pipelines stopped none before execution because they have no pre-execution stage. To find a structural error, Spark had to run the pipeline on a cluster until it reached the broken step.

Across the builds we measured, procedural runs used 596 executor-seconds, compared with 17 for declarative runs. Dry-run validation of declarative code caught structural errors early and reduced compute by 34X.

2. Declarative pipeline code was half the size of procedural pipelines

Among the completed builds, declarative pipelines were about half the size, with a median of 64 lines compared with 131 for procedural pipelines.

The procedural implementations also varied more. For the same job, some used Spark transformations while others loaded the data into memory and processed it one row at a time. Both passed on the test data, but the in-memory version can fail when the data grows. Across the benchmark, 19 procedural builds used this shortcut. None of the declarative builds did.

Shorter, more consistent code gives a team less to review and one pattern to maintain.

3. On logic errors, the two came out level

Those are the two advantages. When running the tests, we also identified two caveats.

First, a dry run can only catch structural mistakes. It cannot catch a silent one: a pipeline that runs cleanly and returns the wrong answer, which is the more dangerous kind. On that count, the two came out even: their silent-error rates were within roughly 15% of each other, a gap too small to be a real difference. Declarative makes structural mistakes cheap to catch; it does nothing for logic, which still needs tests and review.

4. Declarative spends more up front to save more later

Declarative spends more in one place. The agent iterates on the dry run, retrying until the pipeline is sound, so it does more of its thinking in tokens up front rather than discovering problems on a cluster later. The tokens are a fixed, one-time spend, paid while the pipeline is being written; the amount does not change based on your data size or how often the pipeline runs. Wasted cluster compute is the opposite: it recurs on every bad run and grows with the data, so the more you process, the more a bad build costs. Paying a fixed cost up front to avoid one that keeps growing only looks better as your pipelines and data get bigger.

The complete set of measured differences is shown below.

Dimension Procedural PySpark Declarative (SDP)
What the agent produces Code that runs A description that gets checked
Structural errors Surface mid-run, after partial writes, or never; none stopped before output Caught at the dry-run; 55 of 264 stopped before any output
Cost

Cluster time: ~34x higher (up to ~521 executor-seconds on a failed run)

LLM tokens: baseline

Cluster time: baseline (~0.5 executor-seconds on a failed run)

LLM tokens: ~2.3x (median build ≈ $0.50 vs $0.26, Opus 4.8 list rates)
Code size baseline

Lines of code: ~51% fewer (median)

AST size: ~44% smaller
Silent bugs (ran clean, wrong answer) 73 of 264 (27.7%) 85 of 264 (32.2%)

At production scale, the declarative approach comes out ahead. It costs about 2.3 times more in LLM tokens, and in exchange, it never spends cluster time on a pipeline that was never going to work. At production scale, the declarative approach proves advantageous by trading slightly higher LLM token costs for guaranteed prevention of wasted cluster time on failing pipelines. This becomes increasingly cost-effective as data volumes scale, since compute waste grows proportionally while token costs remain constant.

If you are evaluating agents for pipeline work, treat how the agent writes as seriously as which agent you pick. A better agent makes fewer mistakes; a declarative pipeline makes the mistakes cheap and catches them before they cost anything.

The repository documents the design, data, and complete provenance. To get started with your agents using Spark Declarative Pipelines, refer to the official programming guide and use the SDP skill with PySpark.

Do I have to trust the AI agent for this to work?

No, and not having to is the point. The declarative agent only ever writes declarative pipeline code — a description of the tables it wants — and Spark itself checks that description before anything runs. The checker is part of the platform: you are trusting Spark's evaluation of the pipeline, not the model. The agent never runs code or reads your data itself.

Is this only about Spark Declarative Pipelines, or does it apply more broadly?

It applies more broadly to declarative approaches: anywhere you can separate "here is what I want" from "now go build it," so the first part can be checked on its own. You see the same shape in SQL itself, in infrastructure-as-code tools, and in schema-first APIs. Spark Declarative Pipelines is the one we benchmarked, but the reasoning holds for any tool built that way.

The declarative agent uses 2.3x the tokens. Isn't that a dealbreaker?

Not at realistic pipeline sizes. The 2.3x comes to roughly $0.50 in tokens per median declarative build, versus $0.26 for procedural, at Opus 4.8 list rates. One failed procedural run burned about 521 executor-seconds, while a rejected declarative one cost roughly half a second — so avoiding a few bad runs covers a lot of extra tokens, and the gap only widens as data volumes grow. Token prices also move around with whatever model service you use, while compute costs are steadier and easier to plan against.

entries.title: Real-time energy trading and analytics on Databricks
entries.summary: Why does real-time energy trading need more than faster data?Energy trading desks...
entries.content:
See how Databricks combines real-time energy trading, risk monitoring, machine learning, and historical analytics with one platform and one governance model.

by Victoria Sicking and Jack Yallop

  • Energy trading teams often run separate systems for live trading and analytics, creating stale risk data, duplicated governance, and synchronization overhead.
  • Databricks runs this on one platform. Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode streams market data into Lakebase, a Serverless Postgres for apps and agents. That data feeds the live trading app, machine learning models, dashboards and Genie One, a natural-language query tool.
  • Unity Catalog, the Databricks governance layer, controls it all in one place. Permissions, lineage and audit are set up once instead of for each system.

Energy trading desks work in markets where conditions change quickly and decisions are measured in milliseconds. Two changes make this harder: higher price volatility, and the move EU’s day-ahead electricity market move from hourly to 15-minute trading intervals. The 15-minute market time unit is part of the Single-Day Ahead Coupling (SDAC), the system that connects day-ahead electricity markets across EU countries. This creates four times as many market periods per hour and increasing the volume of records, orders, and risk recalculations. Keeping those calculations accurate requires data that is current – which points directly to how data is stored and governed, not only how fast it arrives.

Stale data is more than an inconvenience for a trading desk. It can make risk controls reflect an earlier state of the market, contribute to missed intraday moves, and put desk limits out of sync with current positions.

Many organizations respond with two stacks. An operational system supports the live desk and millisecond transactions. A separate analytical system supports strategy backtesting, machine learning and regulatory reporting. The split matches two different workloads, but it creates four recurring problems:

  • Two versions of the truth
  • A freshness gap in risk controls
  • Duplicated governance and lineage
  • Multiple synchronization pipelines between the different systems

Machine learning adds another dependency. Models need historical data for training, but their outputs must be available in the live trading workflow. Moving models and data between separate systems adds complexity to an already time-sensitive process. The alternative is a unified platform for data, analytics and AI – one that Real-Time Mode streams in with millisecond latency and Lakebase Postgres holds ready – so both the live desk and the model pipeline draw from the same source without an extra transfer step.

Operational and analytical workloads run together by sharing one data foundation. The solution presented below by Victoria Sicking, Solutions Architect at Databricks, described in 'Run Live Energy Trading, Risk, and Analytics in Databricks' below combines six components on the Databricks Data + AI Platform, and the key design choice is that no component maintains its own separate copy of the data. All of them work from what Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode has written into Lakebase and the lakehouse.

  • Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode for continuous event processing with millisecond latency
  • Lakebase, a serverless Postgres for apps and agents, for the operational database
  • Databricks Apps for the live trading interface.
  • Machine learning models for real-time price forecasts and trade signals.
  • Genie One for historical analysis.
  • Unity Catalog for governance across the workflow.

Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode receives market data and streams it into Lakebase, used here as the operational (OLTP) database for millisecond reads, transactions, and upserts. The same data can then support the analytical workloads built on the lakehouse.

Teams no longer need to coordinate parallel pipelines, one for the live desk and another for backtesting and reporting. Time previously burned on reconciliation and coordination is released by creating a single ingestion pathway into your data estate for market and position data. Unity Catalog – the Databricks governance layer for permissions, lineage and audit – applies that governance across the app, business intelligence and machine learning workloads, so they are not configured independently in multiple systems.

It looks like a single application showing prices, positions, profit and loss (P&L) and risk, all updating as the market moves. The live experience is built on Databricks Apps – the way to build and host data applications, such as a live trading interface, on the platform – bringing together what a desk needs to monitor the market and act on changing conditions, served directly from Lakebase so the desk is always reading from the same governed data that feeds the analytical workloads, with no separate operational copy required.

The demo displays instrument prices for Brent crude, German and French power spots, EUR-to-USD conversion, EU carbon allowances (EUAs) and TTF gas.

Risk is monitored against the desk's limits in the same workflow. When a measure approaches a limit, the app raises a risk alert so the desk can see the change and respond immediately. This replaces a nightly batch process that calculates risk from an earlier snapshot of the data.

The application is not a reporting surface disconnected from the data platform. Lakebase provides the operational layer behind the app, and the streaming pipeline keeps the information current.

Train machine learning models on the same governed data that supports the live desk, track their development and lineage with MLflow, and deploy approved versions through Databricks Model Serving. Their outputs can then surface directly in the app.

Energy trading teams need models that can anticipate risk and identify potential trade signals, and running everything on one governed, unified copy of the data removes the handoff between a training system and a live system – the model sees exactly what the desk sees.

The demo shows a real-time price forecast that can contribute to a trade signal. The path between the data used to train a model and the workflow that consumes its output gets shorter. Machine learning becomes part of the end-to-end trading workflow rather than a separate system sitting between the live and analytical stacks.

The same governed data can also support risk analysis and model development. Operational and analytical workloads stay connected, and teams do not need to reconcile separate versions of the data after the fact.

Analysts use an embedded dashboard and Genie One, both built on the same data foundation as the live app. The embedded dashboard presents historical trading data, including total trades, traded volume and comparisons between traders.

For deeper analysis, analysts can use SQL, Python or Spark. They can also use Genie One – the Databricks natural-language interface for asking questions of governed data – without writing the query themselves. In the demo, the analyst asks Genie One to identify the top five counterparties by number of trades and compare total buy volume with sell volume for each.

Genie One works within the Databricks workspace and uses the available data context and defined semantics to answer. Analysts can move from a dashboard view yielding fixed insights to a bespoke analysis of the data while staying in the same governed environment. A unified copy of the data means results agree between the live desk and the analytics back-office.

Data flows from a market feed, through streaming and Lakebase, to the app, analytics and machine learning, all under Unity Catalog governance. Because Unity Catalog spans every component, the permissions, lineage and audit that apply to the live desk also apply to dashboards, Genie One and machine learning – configured once, not reproduced in each system. The steps are:

  • A market feed, such as ICE, APEX or a Kafka stream, provides the source events.
  • Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode processes the incoming data continuously.
  • Lakebase acts as the managed Postgres sink and operational database for the live desk.
  • Teams looking to build analytical layers and run historical analysis or backtesting can now build on that data in the Lakehouse.
  • Databricks Apps uses the operational data to present live prices, positions, P&L, risk, alerts and model outputs.
  • Embedded dashboards and Genie One support historical analysis and questions about trading activity.
  • Machine learning models use the same data to produce price forecasts and trade signals.
  • Unity Catalog applies governance across the app, analytics and machine learning workflows.

The live desk, analytics and machine learning workloads are not separate destinations that need repeated data movement. They are different ways of working with the same governed data.

The question is whether operational and analytical requirements must be served by disconnected systems with separate copies, governance models and synchronization logic. They do have different requirements, but one platform can serve both and consolidating on one governed copy of data means the desk, the risk models and the reporting layer are never out of sync with each other.

When these workloads run on separate systems, risk controls can depend on batch data, models can be trained on information that does not match the live system, and governance, lineage and synchronization pipelines must be maintained more than once.

The Databricks Energy Trading solution brings these capabilities together on one governed data foundation. With this setup, teams can evaluate risk as the market moves while using the same governed data for P&L, exposure, backtesting, machine learning, dashboards and natural-language analysis.

To learn more about how you can get started, visit:

Separate systems can create two versions of the truth, a freshness gap in risk controls, duplicated governance and lineage, extra maintenance work, and additional synchronization pipelines between systems. Machine learning also becomes harder to manage when models are trained on one system but must run on another. Maintaining one governed and unified copy of the data, with a single set of controls, removes most of these costs.

Energy trading teams can run the live desk, risk, machine learning and historical analytics on one governed copy of data in Databricks. Spark Structured Streaming Real-Time Mode, Lakebase, Databricks Apps and Unity Catalog replace the second system and the duplicate controls.

Lakebase is a fully managed Postgres database native to the Databricks Data + AI Platform, used here as the operational (OLTP) database for millisecond reads, transactions and upserts. Because it sits within the same platform as the lakehouse, it connects operational data with analytical workloads on one governed and unified copy of the data rather than requiring a separate database outside the platform.

A live trading application built on Databricks Apps, the way to build and host data applications, such as a live trading interface, on the platform, can display prices, positions, P&L and risk as they update. Risk alerts trigger as measures approach desk limits, so traders respond to current conditions instead of relying only on batch calculations.

Unity Catalog is the Databricks governance layer for permissions, lineage and audit, providing one governance layer across the operational application, analytics and machine learning workflows. It maintains centralized permissions, lineage and audit end to end, so teams configure controls once for the single copy of data rather than reproducing separate governance for each system.

entries.content:
How to measure and manage AI costs.

  • Enterprises are shifting from "tokenmaxxing" to "valuemaxxing," measuring the impact generated per dollar spent on AI.
  • Measuring AI ROI requires attribution granular enough to trace spend to a user, team, project or even a single pull request
  • Spend guardrails, end-to-end observability and a centralized point all AI traffic flows through are the foundation teams need now

For the past two years, the story around enterprise AI adoption has mostly been about getting people to use it. Over the past few months, that story has rapidly been changing in many organizations. AI observability that once measured success by token volume is starting to measure success by return on investment, and the enterprises that figure out cost management first are the ones that will be able to scale AI without their spend outrunning their revenue.

At its core, AI cost management is the practice of measuring, attributing, controlling and optimizing AI spend across models, agents, applications and teams. The goal isn't simply to use fewer tokens, but to maximize the business value generated for every dollar spent. As AI agents take on more autonomous work, that discipline increasingly extends to managing the cost of agent reasoning, tool calls, and the models powering them.

We sat down with Kevin Stumpf, a Senior Staff Engineer at Databricks and Technical Lead for Unity Gateway, to talk through how teams should actually put that discipline into practice: not treating AI cost as a line item to minimize, but as a system to manage.

Social media is full of leaders arguing that "tokenmaxxing," running AI as hard and as often as possible, is the right way to accelerate innovation. Other than the obvious cost implications, why is that the wrong way to think about AI adoption?

Kevin Stumpf: The industry is moving from tokenmaxxing to valuemaxxing. In the early days, there were public leaderboards showing how many tokens people were burning through, and that made sense as a strategy at the time. A lot of people were reluctant to start using AI, so showing that the leaders everyone looked up to were heavy AI users gave others a reason to follow. If I see someone I respect using a ton of AI, I want to be like that person.

But the system got gamed. Once being at the top of the leaderboard became a status symbol, people figured out the fastest way to get there wasn't good work, it was volume. Spin up a dumb agent that runs in a loop, have it ask what the weather is over and over, and burn through tokens doing essentially nothing. That was the predictable outcome of an incentive structure that rewarded raw usage instead of outcomes.

Now that organizations are broadly bought into AI, the conversation has shifted to responsible, effective use. What we should really be building toward is a different kind of leaderboard, one that ranks people by the impact they generated with AI divided by what it cost to generate it. That's return on investment, and it's a much harder thing to quantify than raw token counts, but it's the number that actually matters. Related: What’s Driving Enterprise AI Adoption?

Can you walk us through what "cost attribution" really means in AI?

Kevin Stumpf: AI cost attribution is ultimately about answering two questions: where does my spend come from, and what did I get for it? At the simplest level, that means attributing cost to an individual user or a team, like a data science team or a software engineering team. It can also map to a specific project, or to a node in an org chart, like understanding how much spend sits under a VP of AI versus an SVP of engineering.

The goal is granular enough visibility that you can slice and dice the data and understand where cost is actually coming from, because you can't manage what you can't measure. Databricks provides cost attribution out of the box by user, group, agent, AI gateway endpoint, model, provider and time period. But organizations can also hyper-customize it using request-level tags. A tag can represent anything your organization cares about, like a specific pull request, a feature or an external customer, and once every request carries that tag, you can aggregate spend against it however you need to.

That shift in customer sentiment has been real. Six months ago, the top concern was falling behind on AI adoption. Now it's the opposite: AI is often used for silly things, costs are growing faster than revenue, and leaders are asking how to bend that cost curve before it eats into profitability. This isn't a hypothetical. It's a boardroom-level conversation at nearly every organization we talk to, including internally at Databricks.

Token usage and context window size get blamed a lot, but are rarely explained well. What does context bloat actually look like in a production system, and what's the practical fix?

Kevin Stumpf: Context bloat means throwing far more information at an agent than it needs to make a good decision. That's a problem for two reasons. First, it burns unnecessary tokens. Second, it's distracting: the agent has to process that extra information and decide whether it's relevant, which is its own kind of overhead. It's not unlike handing a person a stack of irrelevant documents and asking them to figure out what matters before they can even start the task.

The best fix isn't trimming or caching after the fact, it's not generating the bloat in the first place. A common and effective pattern is letting the agent pull relevant context on demand, through tools, MCP servers or skills, rather than proactively pushing everything it might need up front. You should only push context to an agent by default if you're 90% certain or more that it's genuinely important for the task at hand. Otherwise, let the agent know what's available and allow it to fetch what it needs when it needs it.

Model selection is often a "pick once" decision. Why should it be dynamic instead, and how does intelligent routing decide, in real time, whether a task needs a frontier model or something cheaper and faster? Does that same idea extend to choosing between different agent harnesses?

Kevin Stumpf: AI cost optimization isn't about always choosing the cheapest model, and teams should shift to choosing the lowest-cost model or harness that can deliver the quality a task requires. The reality right now is that frontier models are highly capable and expensive, while non-frontier models are still very capable, just less expensive. Roughly 5 to 10% of tasks genuinely need a frontier model, either because the stakes are high enough that you want the best possible outcome, or because the problem is too complex for anything less. The other 90% of tasks are solvable by lesser models, whether that's open source models you host yourself or cheaper model families from the major labs.

Left to their own incentives, most employees will default to the most expensive model available, because their goal is simply to get the problem solved, and nobody is watching what it costs them individually. Smart Routing solves that by inserting a layer that assesses task complexity in real time and decides whether a request should go to a frontier model or a lower-cost one, with the goal of maintaining the same quality output at a lower cost.

Harness routing is the next layer beyond model routing. There's emerging research showing that the exact same model, run through a different harness, can produce meaningfully different costs. That makes sense, because the harness determines how the model interacts with its environment: what rules it follows, when it compacts the context window, what business logic governs its behavior. All of that directly affects how many tokens get spent. Harness routing is the next step in that crawl-walk-run evolution of cost optimization, which we enable through Unity Gateway and Omnigent, our meta-harness.

Let's talk about guardrails on spend itself, like hard caps, budgets, and rate limits. What's the right way to design these so they stop runaway costs without hurting developer productivity or breaking production workflows?

Kevin Stumpf: Some rules apply to every organization, and others depend on the use case or the company. Everyone should have hard spend caps in place to catch runaway usage. If your typical power user spends around $300 a day on AI at most, set the hard cap somewhat above that, maybe $500. That gap gives you room to catch genuine errors, like an agent that got left running in a loop by accident, without capping off legitimate high-usage days.

Beyond that baseline, differentiated budgets by team or project make a lot of sense. A team working on something critical for the CEO might warrant a much higher budget than a team working on lower-priority work, and that decision should weigh the value of what that team produces against the cost of giving them more headroom.

Budgets should also be able to trigger different types of responses, not just a hard stop. They can send alerts, apply hard caps or reduce available model capacity, for example cutting off default access to frontier models once a team has burned through 70% of its budget and routing the rest of their requests to open source models instead. The core principles that apply everywhere: prevent runaway spend, set differentiated limits by group or project, alert before you cap and build in intelligent capacity reduction rather than an abrupt shutoff.

REPORT

The agentic AI playbook for the enterprise

Which platforms offer agent monitoring and cost tracking together, and how far can that visibility take you toward measuring actual ROI, not just spend?

Kevin Stumpf: Measuring cost is a lot easier than connecting that cost to return on investment, and that's the question everyone wants answered and almost nobody has fully solved yet. Session or request-level tagging is what makes this possible. If an agent is working on a specific pull request, it can tag its session or specific requests it generates with that pull request's identifier. That attribution flows back into a cost dashboard, so you can see, for example, that a given pull request cost $300 to complete. This is something we’re already doing internally at Databricks.

In an ideal state, and this is something we're building into the Unity Gateway product. You can go a step further and connect that pull request to a specific feature, and that feature to a measurable outcome, like how much revenue or pipeline it generated in a given period. That's the holy grail: not just knowing what AI cost, but knowing what it returned. With Unity Gateway, we already have a highly customizable platform to build this on, and we're investing in making that cost-to-return view available out of the box rather than something teams have to construct themselves.

For a company running multiple models, agents and tools across many teams, what does good spend visibility actually require? Is it a dashboard problem, a governance problem or a FinOps problem?

Kevin Stumpf: Good spend visibility requires that every AI interaction flows through a centralized system. That's what allows you to lock down the right information consistently, so you can build reliable dashboards and alerts on top of it. An AI gateway provides a centralized control point for AI cost management across models, agents, tools and teams. Databricks Unity Gateway is designed to provide that centralized control point across models, agents, tools and coding agents. When AI interactions flow through a common control point, organizations can observe usage, attribute costs, enforce budgets and optimize spend in one place.

But having the centralized system isn't enough on its own. You also need a way to enforce that everyone actually routes their AI traffic through it. Visibility only works if adoption is universal, not optional.

Cost control can't come at the expense of quality or reliability. How do you know when an optimization has gone too far and started hurting output?

Kevin Stumpf: That's genuinely use case specific. You need a feedback mechanism, and it can be either subjective or objective. Subjective feedback is anecdotal, someone on the team telling you they can't get the job done within the current budget. That's fast to get but easy to dismiss as one person's complaint. Objective feedback comes from automated evaluations, which are harder to set up but far more reliable.

For a common use case like coding agents, that might mean defining a proxy metric for quality, such as merged pull requests that don't get rolled back within two weeks. From there, you can experiment: cut the budget in half and see whether that gold star metric moves, holds steady or even improves, since constraints sometimes breed creativity. Running parallel experiments across teams with different budgets, models and harnesses, or time-bound comparisons over a few weeks, lets you infer whether a given budget is creating value or destroying it, rather than guessing.

What role does end-to-end tracing and monitoring play here? Once you can see prompts, tool calls and token usage across an entire agent workflow, what does that unlock that you couldn't do before?

Kevin Stumpf: Tracing is about collecting the full exhaust of what agents are doing: what they're thinking, what tools they're calling, what data they're pulling in, whether the prompts are good or bad. That raw data is what you can mine for insight, whether that's identifying abuse, waste, security leaks or simply patterns you never thought to look for.

This mirrors what happened in the broader data industry. Early on, we only had clean, structured data in databases. Then came data lakes, which for a while became data swamps because people dumped unstructured data into them without a way to extract value from it. Eventually those swamps turned back into usable data lakes, and now we're in a better position than ever to extract insight from unstructured and semi-structured data, largely because LLMs are flexible enough to process it. Agent traces fall into that same category. The more of it you collect, the more insight becomes available, and it's easier to get to than it's ever been.

A lot of enterprises are moving from single AI applications to fleets of agents. Does that shift change the cost equation (new cost drivers? new blind spots?) compared to running one model behind one app?

Kevin Stumpf: It doesn't change the equation so much as it multiplies it. Agent swarms are going to be the new reality, and every one of those agents will be spending tokens that need to be attributed, monitored and managed. Right now is the time to put the right cost visibility and management foundation in place, before the number of agents in production grows the way it's projected to.

Coding agents are the dominant category burning tokens today, but that's going to expand into many other classes of agents doing autonomous work around the clock, agents calling other agents calling other agents. Organizations that wait to build centralized AI observability and cost management infrastructure until that complexity arrives will be building it under pressure, instead of on their own terms.

If you had to leave enterprise AI leaders with one mindset shift about cost management heading into next year, what would it be?

Kevin Stumpf: I wouldn't wait for next year. This is urgent, and it should be treated that way starting now. If I had to boil it down to a single idea, it's this: you can't manage what you don't measure. That applies to raw materials, it applies to people, and it applies to AI just as much. AI is quickly becoming one of the most important line items on a company's cash flow statement, and it needs to be fully instrumented so it can be measured and, in turn, managed. It's just another raw ingredient in the system that produces your organization's goods or services, and it deserves to be treated with the same discipline.

The clock starts now Controlling AI costs across teams using multiple models and tools isn't a problem that gets solved with a single dashboard or a one-time model choice. It's an operating discipline: attribution granular enough to trace spend to a person or a project, routing that adapts in real time to what a task requires, guardrails that catch runaway spend before it becomes a headline and tracing detailed enough to turn raw usage data into real insight. The organizations getting ahead of this aren't the ones spending the least on AI. They're the ones who can say, with confidence, exactly what they got for what they spent.

entries.content:
Augmenting your first line of defense with knowledge, tools and context.

by Razi Bayati and Anthony Melnick

  • As fraudsters use agentic AI to attack at machine speed, defense teams must accelerate response times using AI coworkers. Additionally, real-time network telemetry can be used as fraud signals and improve fraud detection models.
  • Databricks unifies Fraud detection stack on a single platform: Lakebase removes the analytical and transactional split for faster data sync, Databricks Apps powers a custom case-management workbench, and Genie as an AI coworker, provides natural-language querying over governed fraud data; This unified stack supports fraud detection team to work more efficiently against fraudsters.
  • Our Telecom Fraud Prevention Solution Accelerator deploys this entire pipeline, risk engine, workbench, and AI investigation agent into your workspace via Databricks Asset Bundles, adaptable to other industries.

Background

According to the Communications Fraud Control Association's 2025 survey, telecom fraud losses have climbed to $41.82 billion1, and the broader fraud economy is growing fast: U.S. consumers alone reported losing more than $12.5 billion to fraud in 2024, a 25% jump in a single year2. Breaches are getting more expensive too; the global average cost of a data breach hit a record $4.88 million in 20243; Every dollar of fraud costs a carrier roughly 3.4x once you count chargebacks, replacement costs, and the operational overhead of investigating it.

A telecom account is no longer just a phone plan. It's the gateway to many assets that a subscriber owns: banking apps authenticate through phone number, password resets flow through it, and two-factor codes land on it. Consequently, when a fraudster compromises an account through phishing, social engineering, or using credentials from an old breach, the clock runs fast. Within minutes they can execute a SIM swap, change the billing address, order expensive devices, and pivot into linked financial accounts often before the victim or the carrier notices anything at all. Meanwhile, the fraud team is still waiting on last night's batch job to complete.

That dichotomy, fraud moving at machine speed while detection moves at batch speed, is the inhibitor. For an executive team, fraud is not a security footnote. It’s revenue leakage, regulatory exposure, accelerated churn, and an operations tax that rarely shows up cleanly in a loss report. Every major fraud type succeeds for one of three reasons:

  • It creates a data signature that has not been detected in time
  • It exploits gaps between systems that don't talk to each other
  • Or it thrives in the lag of batch processing.

Here's the reframe we think matters most: All three are data architecture problems that can be solved with a unified, real-time, governed data foundation.

Account takeover and SIM swap attacks were up 240% in 2024 in Australia based on stockhead , and roughly 90% of them now happen with no contact with the actual victim. The fraudster's request simply looks legitimate. International Revenue Share Fraud pumps $4–7 billion a year into premium-rate numbers by looking like normal traffic. SIM box bypass fraud (~$3.1B/year) hides inside call patterns that seem routine1.

In nearly every case, the signal that would detect this fraud already exists - it's just split across the six or seven systems (CDRs, CRM, billing, device/SIM, network, digital channel logs) that don't share a single query surface. Often sophisticated fraud types are processed in overnight batches when the attack window is measured in minutes while simpler fraud types such as spoofing can be caught real time.

The human cost of that fragmentation compounds the financial one. Rigid rule-based systems flood analysts with false positives, so fraud teams spend hours investigating benign account changes while the sophisticated attacks executing at machine speed slip through. It's a daunting cycle: analysts drowning in alerts, genuine threats going undetected, losses mounting.

Most operators have invested heavily in fraud management systems that successfully block the known, well-understood attack patterns, and those systems are saving real money today. The opportunity isn't to rip those out, it's to augment them. But fraud is an adversarial game, not a static one — every pattern a model learns to catch is a pattern fraudsters are actively working to route around, and they do it fast. The gaps show up in exactly what existing fraud engines were never built for: cross-channel correlation, behavioral modeling, device emulation, and fraud patterns that evolve faster than a rule-change cycle can keep up with. Those gaps trace back to architecture, not effort — and architecture that can't move at the speed of the adversary is architecture that's already behind.

The common thread in any anti-fraud system is that it will undergo adversarial drift, and it will happen on the fraudster's timeline, not yours. The moment a fraudster gets caught, they change behavior immediately — no delay, no courtesy window. That means the recall of any deployed model starts degrading right away, sometimes within 24 hours. In this environment, being outdated isn't a minor inefficiency, it's the difference between a model that catches fraud and one that's effectively blind to it. There is no such thing as "good enough for now" — a detection system is only as good as its last update, and the agility of the monitor-tune-redeploy loop isn't a nice-to-have, it's the whole game.

This is exactly where most fraud operations lose the race. The typical pattern: an operational (OLTP) system handles live transactions, while a separate analytical (OLAP) system houses the actual intelligence: — the context, the historical queries, the fraud models, the dashboards data scientists refine every day. The problem is that the live risk engine can't reach into that analytical environment fast enough at decision time. Teams must then fall back on a slow, costly synchronization process — scheduled batch jobs that copy finished "gold" data (engineered features, model scores, risk signals) out of the OLAP warehouse and back into the operational database.

That copying is the bottleneck, and in an adversarial-drift world, bottlenecks are where you lose. The operational store is always working off a stale snapshot — and "stale" compounds fast when your adversary is actively mutating behavior hour by hour. The pipeline is brittle (a schema change upstream breaks it), expensive to maintain, and worst of all, slow to repair;every hour it's down is an hour your decision engine is running on yesterday's intelligence against today's attack. The models and context that make detection smart end up stranded one hop away from the decision engine, exactly when speed matters most.

Put an AI agent on top and it inherits the same gap, just with higher stakes: either it reasons without the rich OLAP context it needs — fast but blind — or you copy sensitive gold data out to reach it, trading governance for access. Neither option holds up against an adversary that's already moved on by the time your architecture catches up.

The fix has to attack the actual bottleneck: the hop between where intelligence lives and where decisions get made. Lakebase, our managed Postgres engine integrated into the unified environment, eliminates the traditional OLTP/OLAP split entirely. Gold tables in the lakehouse sync continuously into Lakebase, giving the real-time scoring engine sub-millisecond feature retrieval — right alongside the same analytical models that generated them. There's no batch job standing between the decision engine and the intelligence it needs, which means no stale snapshot and no brittle pipeline waiting to break on the next schema change. When a model starts drifting, the fix propagates at the speed the drift demands, not at the speed of the next scheduled sync.

Meanwhile, our agentic platform and Genie let analysts analyze historical incidents, synthesize operational playbooks, and automate complex investigative work — closing the monitor-tune-redeploy loop faster, so the gap between "fraudster changes behavior" and "model adapts" shrinks from days to something much closer to real time. With Databricks Apps, teams can rapidly deploy custom operational tools on this same unified architecture, instead of waiting on a separate build cycle every time a new fraud pattern demands a new tool.

And because it's one architecture rather than two systems stitched together, an AI agent built on top doesn't face the earlier trade-off between reasoning with rich context and preserving governance. A single plane under Unity Catalog manages governance, lineage, and security from raw network ingestion through to the live transaction decision — so speed and control stop being opposites. Compliance leaders get full lineage, engineering teams get an architecture that can actually keep pace with an adversary that doesn't wait around.

Databricks built a Solution Accelerator for telecom fraud, covering the full lifecycle from raw data to an analyst queue to the executive dashboard.

The pipeline. The solution includes a pipeline with a medallion architecture (Bronze → Silver → Gold) that generates realistic transaction, device, and network Call Detail Record data at scale.

Additionally, a risk engine scores every transaction against rules like impossible travel, cell/IP mismatch, rapid cell-tower hops, roaming anomalies, and device emulation, the same category of signals that catch SIM box and SIM-swap fraud in production. Score threshold route transactions to one of three outcomes: auto-approve, queue for analyst review, or auto-block.

The fraud analyst workbench app showcases different fraud workflows with three role-based views built on the same governed data:

  • Executive - financial P&L impact, quarterly trends, regional risk distribution, and a Genie Space for a leader to ask questions in natural language like "which regions had the most SIM-swap cases this quarter?" and get governed, data-backed answers - no analyst or SQL required.
  • Management - Ticket pipeline health, a 30-day AI forecast, fraud engine performance, and SLA tracking, so managers can staff analyst capacity proactively instead of reactively.
  • Analyst - a case queue and device/case detail view backed by a tool-calling AI investigation Genie agent that reads case history, risk rules, and policy together, then recommends approve, deny, or escalate - and a Knowledge Assistant trained on the company's fraud playbook for procedural questions like escalation thresholds and documentation standards.

None of the individual pieces here - a risk-scoring pipeline, an AI agent, a governed catalog - are unique. What's different is running all of them on one platform instead of stitching together a fraud engine, a separate feature store, a BI tool, and a bolted-on AI layer, each with its own governance model and its own latency tax. For telecom operators, the opportunity is huge. It's recognizing that the infrastructure built to protect the business is the same infrastructure that can turn network data into a new revenue line.

  • Clone it, deploy the pipeline, and stand up the analyst workbench in your own workspace - the industry-specific logic lives in a single configuration file, so the same architecture retargets to fintech, insurance, or e-commerce fraud with no changes to the core platform.
  • To go deeper, reach out to your Databricks account team to provision Lakebase, creating synced tables, configuring a fraud-domain Genie Space, and building the investigation app.
